title: Green economy

definition.text: An economy that tries to cut environmental risks and ecological scarcities and to develop sustainably without degrading the environment.

facts.text: It is closely related to ecological economics but has a more politically applied focus.
UNEP says a green economy must be fair as well as efficient, including a just transition to a low-carbon, resource-efficient and socially inclusive economy.
What sets it apart from earlier economic regimes is treating natural capital and ecological services as having economic value, with costs pushed onto society traced back to whoever causes them.
Green economies need a shift to renewable energy to replace fossil fuels, plus energy conservation and efficient energy use.
UNEP's 2011 Green Economy Report put the yearly financing needed to green the global economy at US$1.05 to US$2.59 trillion, about one-tenth of total global investment per year.
The green economy chiefly concerns land-based activities, while the related blue economy applies sustainability to oceans, seas and coasts.
Critics argue that mainstream versions relying on price mechanisms to protect nature will extend corporate control into areas from forestry to water.
Ecological economist Clive Spash argued that the UN's Green Economy is not a new approach and diverts attention from the real drivers of environmental crisis.

contested_note: Critics dispute whether market-based green economy policies can address the real causes of environmental crisis.

definition.text: Any economic theory that treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem it sits within.

facts.text: It usually takes a holistic approach, mixing economic ideas with other subjects depending on the theorist.
Some economists treat it as a branch of established schools, for example classical economics with the old factor 'land' widened into natural capital.
UNEP's growing commitment to natural capital and full cost accounting under the 'green economy' banner could blur the lines between schools.

definition.text: Indicators built to measure how green an economy is, from human ecological impact to efficiency and green investment flows.

facts.text: Ordinary economic output and progress are measured with economic index indicators; green indices arose to capture human ecological impact as well.
The Global Green Economy Index measures green economic performance and perceptions of it in 130 countries along four dimensions.
Ecological footprint measurements are another standard used by municipal governments to gauge human impact.

title: Degrowth

definition.text: An academic and social movement, mainly in Europe, that calls for planned, democratic reduction of production and consumption to tackle social and ecological crises.

facts.text: Common policy goals include shrinking humanity's environmental impact, redistributing income and wealth within and between countries, and moving from materialistic values toward a convivial, participatory society.
It rejects growth in GDP as a measure of human and economic development, arguing that capitalism's focus on growth causes wide ecological damage and is not needed to raise living standards.
Degrowth writers argue that absolute decoupling of GDP from resource use and emissions is only possible for short periods, in specific places, or with small mitigation rates.
It warns that efficiency technologies can trigger the rebound effect, also called the Jevons paradox, cancelling out expected resource savings.
The movement names economist Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen as its main intellectual inspiration; the French term décroissance was used for a 1979 translation of his essays.
The first international degrowth conference was held in Paris in 2008.
Critics call it vague, say it ignores rebound effects and lacks political support, and argue environmental taxes or tradable permits work much better.
Critics also note that far-reaching degrowth scenarios are projected to raise extreme poverty.

contested_note: Supporters say degrowth would improve living standards and protect ecosystems, while critics argue it is vague, politically unpopular and likely to raise poverty.

definition.text: The concrete measures degrowth writers propose for shrinking production and consumption fairly.

facts.text: A 2022 survey of degrowth literature from 2005 to 2020 found 530 specific policy proposals.

The ten most cited were universal basic income, shorter working time, job guarantees with a living wage, maximum income caps, declining caps on resource use and emissions, not-for-profit cooperatives, deliberative forums, reclaiming the commons, ecovillages and housing cooperatives.
In a Swedish survey, reduced working hours got about 50% support, a wealth tax 40%, a meat tax 30%, a maximum income 25% and a basic income 15%.

title: Growth versus environment debate

definition.text: The dispute over whether economic growth can be made compatible with environmental sustainability, with positions ranging from green growth through agrowth to degrowth.

facts.text: Green growth holds growth and sustainability compatible; agrowth is agnostic about growth and focuses on cutting environmental harm with effective instruments whether the economy grows or shrinks.
In a survey of academics publishing on the topic, under 1% favoured growth at all costs, 42% green growth, 31% agrowth and 17% degrowth.
Another survey of nearly 800 climate policy researchers found 28% support degrowth.
Critics of green growth point instead to frameworks such as the circular economy, steady-state economy, degrowth and doughnut economics.
A 2020 paper argued that changing economic paradigms is essential to prevent environmental destruction, listing options from reformist agrowth to radical degrowth, eco-socialism and eco-anarchism.

contested_note: Researchers are split on whether growth can continue while environmental pressures fall fast enough.
notes: No own article; passes curriculum test 5 (discussed on Degrowth, Green economy, Agrowth and Green growth pages).
